meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a coherent and methodologically sound contribution with novel theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics) and practical advantages (zero-shot phrase representation, interpretability). However, several claims require clarification or additional evidence before publication: (1) The zero-shot claim must be reframed to distinguish phrase representation (zero-shot) from classification (supervised); (2) The horseshoe phenomenon requires independent validation on held-out test set or cross-dataset evaluation; (3) The weak individual geometric features require ablation studies and non-linear classifier comparison to validate geometric meaningfulness; (4) The comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 must be conducted on fair dataset (either full or reduced); (5) The theoretical positioning against conceptual mapping should be empirically validated through human evaluation or processing data comparison. The paper is suitable for publication with major revisions addressing these issues. The contribution is incremental methodologically but potentially disruptive theoretically, depending on validation of the pragmatic/cognitive linguistic framing. The work would benefit from cross-dataset evaluation and human studies to strengthen claims about metaphor as a dynamic contextual phenomenon.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a controlled but substantive contribution to metaphor identification research. To strengthen the work, address the following: (1) ZERO-SHOT CLAIM: Clarify that phrase representation is zero-shot but classification is supervised. Conduct explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases (not just cross-validation folds) to validate true zero-shot capability. (2) GEOMETRIC INTERPRETABILITY: Conduct ablation studies removing individual features to assess their contribution. Test non-linear classifiers (SVM, random forest) to determine whether weak individual features reflect genuine relationships or model limitation. Provide feature importance analysis (SHAP values) to clarify which geometric properties drive predictions. (3) HORSESHOE PHENOMENON: Validate on independent dataset (other metaphor corpus or held-out test set). Provide a priori theoretical justification for why horseshoe should emerge from pragmatic/cognitive linguistic principles. Conduct statistical significance testing of the trend. (4) COMPARISON TO BASELINES: Obtain full-dataset Gutiérrez et al. V2 results or conduct fair reduced-dataset comparison. Report confidence intervals and effect sizes for all comparisons. (5) THEORETICAL VALIDATION: Conduct human evaluation comparing model predictions to human metaphoricity judgments. Test whether pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory better predicts human behavior than conceptual mapping. (6) GENERALIZATION: Evaluate on additional metaphor datasets (VU Amsterdam, TroFi) and linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun). Report performance across dataset types. (7) STATISTICAL REPORTING: Report inter-annotator agreement for Gutiérrez et al. dataset. Provide detailed methodology for χ² test. Report confidence intervals and effect sizes. (8) ALTERNATIVE METHODS: Compare to GloVe, FastText, and contextual embeddings (BERT). Compare to non-linear classifiers. These revisions would significantly strengthen the empirical support for your claims and clarify the scope and limitations of your contribution.
transparency_report: Five specialist reviewers with distinct cognitive roles (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive, claim_verifier) were applied to the paper. Each reviewer operated within their assigned epistemic variant and did not recommend accept/reject decisions.

Reviewers converged on identifying the same core issues: (1) zero-shot claim is misleading, (2) horseshoe phenomenon is post-hoc without validation, (3) most individual geometric features perform poorly, (4) comparison to V2 is indirect, (5) no cross-dataset evaluation. This convergence across diverse cognitive roles suggests these are robust concerns, not artifacts of particular analytical perspectives.

Reviewers diverged on severity and implications of these issues. Structure_analyst emphasizes logical tensions; methodology_auditor emphasizes statistical rigor; novelty assessors diverge on whether contribution is incremental or disruptive; claim_verifier emphasizes evidence gaps. This controlled disagreement reflects legitimate differences in how to weight methodological rigor, novelty, and empirical support.

The paper's theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics vs. conceptual mapping) is novel and coherent but not empirically validated. Reviewers agree this is a gap but differ on whether it is critical flaw (reviewer_2, reviewer_5) or expected limitation for theoretical positioning (reviewer_4). The editor should decide whether empirical validation of theoretical claims is required for publication.

The horseshoe phenomenon is treated as intriguing but uncertain by all reviewers. The post-hoc discovery without a priori prediction raises questions about generalization, but does not invalidate the finding. Independent validation on held-out data or cross-dataset evaluation would clarify whether this is a genuine linguistic principle or dataset-specific artifact.

The weak individual geometric features (most F≈0.64–0.75 vs. baseline 0.697) are flagged by all reviewers as undermining the interpretability claim. However, reviewers differ on implications: some treat this as evidence that combined model reflects logistic regression weighting rather than geometric meaningfulness; others suggest feature interactions might explain combined success. Ablation studies would clarify this.

The zero-shot claim is flagged by all reviewers as misleading because it conflates phrase representation (zero-shot) with classification (supervised). This is a clarity/framing issue, not a validity issue. Clarification and explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases would resolve this concern.

The comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 is flagged by all reviewers as indirect because V2 results are on reduced dataset while V1 results are on full dataset. Authors acknowledge V2 full-dataset performance is likely lower than reported 0.793. This is a methodological concern about fair comparison, not a validity concern about the proposed method.

Retrieved literature (Li et al., TACL) on metaphor recognition emphasizes data-driven and knowledge-base approaches but does not directly address the pragmatic/cognitive linguistic framing or geometric interpretability claims. This reflects the novelty of the paper's theoretical positioning but also suggests limited precedent for validating the approach.

The paper's scope is limited to adjective-noun phrases on a single dataset. No cross-dataset evaluation or evaluation on other linguistic constructions is provided. This is a significant limitation for claims about metaphor as a general linguistic phenomenon.

Statistical reporting is incomplete: no confidence intervals, effect sizes, or detailed methodology for the χ² test; no inter-annotator agreement metrics for the Gutiérrez et al. dataset. This limits the ability to assess practical significance and annotation quality.

The paper demonstrates honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings (e.g., authors acknowledge initial surprise at horseshoe phenomenon, acknowledge V2 comparison is indirect). This transparency is commendable but does not fully resolve the underlying issues.
epistemic_limits: THEORETICAL VALIDATION: The paper's theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics vs. conceptual mapping) cannot be fully validated without direct comparison to human processing data, psycholinguistic experiments, or explicit tests of which theory better predicts human metaphor judgments. The current work provides coherent theoretical motivation but not empirical validation.

GENERALIZATION SCOPE: The evaluation is limited to adjective-noun phrases on a single dataset (Gutiérrez et al. 2016). Generalization to other metaphor types (verb-noun, noun-noun), linguistic constructions, languages, and datasets is unknown. Claims about metaphor as a general linguistic phenomenon cannot be fully supported without cross-dataset evaluation.

GEOMETRIC INTERPRETABILITY: The weak individual geometric features (most F≈0.64–0.75) raise questions about whether the combined model's success reflects genuine geometric meaningfulness or logistic regression's ability to weight weak signals. Ablation studies and non-linear classifier comparison would clarify this, but the current work cannot definitively establish geometric interpretability.

HORSESHOE PHENOMENON CAUSALITY: The horseshoe pattern is discovered post-hoc without a priori prediction or independent validation. The pattern could reflect a genuine linguistic principle, a dataset-specific artifact, or an artifact of the geometric construction. Independent validation on held-out data or cross-dataset evaluation is required to distinguish these possibilities.

ZERO-SHOT CAPABILITY SCOPE: The paper claims zero-shot capability, but evaluation uses cross-validation folds of the same dataset. True zero-shot capability would require evaluation on held-out unseen phrases not in the training set. The current work cannot definitively establish the scope of zero-shot capability.

COMPARISON FAIRNESS: The comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 is indirect because V2 results are on reduced dataset while V1 results are on full dataset. Without full-dataset V2 results or fair reduced-dataset comparison, the relative performance of the proposed method cannot be definitively established.

ANNOTATION QUALITY: No inter-annotator agreement metrics are provided for the Gutiérrez et al. dataset. If annotations are noisy or reflect disagreement, the model's performance ceiling is lower than reported. The current work cannot assess how annotation quality affects results.

ALTERNATIVE METHODS: The paper does not compare to alternative distributional methods (GloVe, FastText, contextual embeddings) or non-linear classifiers (SVM, random forest). Without such comparisons, the relative strength of the proposed approach cannot be definitively established.

PRAGMATIC REASONING ALIGNMENT: The paper claims to operationalize pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory, but does not validate that the model's geometric representations align with human pragmatic reasoning or conceptual organization. The current work cannot establish whether the model captures pragmatic principles or merely statistical patterns.

DATASET BIAS: The Gutiérrez et al. dataset is specifically designed with 23 adjectives chosen for metaphoric/literal versatility. The BO (noun norm) feature's predictiveness may reflect this dataset design rather than a fundamental linguistic property. Evaluation on more balanced datasets would clarify this.

STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The paper reports p<0.05 significance using χ² but provides no confidence intervals, effect sizes, or detailed methodology. The practical significance of the performance improvements (F=0.813 vs. V1=0.817) is unclear without effect size reporting.

FEATURE INTERACTION EFFECTS: The weak individual geometric features but strong combined model suggests feature interactions may be important. However, the paper does not analyze feature interactions or provide insights into how features combine to predict metaphoricity. The mechanism of the combined model's success remains unclear.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes a geometric, context-sensitive distributional semantic model for metaphor identification in adjective-noun phrases, grounded in pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory rather than conceptual mapping frameworks. The core contribution is using contextually-projected geometric subspaces of word vectors to extract features for logistic regression classification, achieving F-score 0.813 (comparable to Gutiérrez et al. V1: 0.817). The paper claims zero-shot capability, geometric interpretability, and discovery of a 'horseshoe phenomenon' where metaphoric and literal phrases cluster geometrically with ambiguous cases in between. Five specialist reviewers with distinct cognitive roles converge on identifying critical gaps between claims and evidence: (1) the zero-shot claim conflates phrase representation (zero-shot) with classification (supervised on labeled data); (2) the horseshoe phenomenon is discovered post-hoc without a priori prediction or independent validation; (3) most individual geometric features perform poorly (F≈0.64–0.75 vs. baseline 0.697), raising questions about whether combined model success reflects geometric meaningfulness or logistic regression weighting; (4) the comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 is indirect (reduced dataset; full-dataset performance unknown); (5) no cross-dataset evaluation limits generalization claims; (6) theoretical positioning against conceptual mapping is asserted but not empirically validated against human processing data. The paper is methodologically sound and theoretically coherent, but empirically underdeveloped in key areas. The contribution is incremental methodologically but potentially disruptive theoretically, contingent on validation of pragmatic/cognitive linguistic framing.
strengths: Coherent theoretical motivation grounded in pragmatic/cognitive linguistics (Wilson & Sperber, Carston, Davidson) with explicit rejection of conceptual mapping as sole framework; well-articulated positioning against dominant Lakoff & Johnson tradition.

Methodologically simple and interpretable geometric framework using triangulation in contextual subspaces; clear mathematical formulation (Equation 1) and explicit operationalization of three desiderata (contextual selection, independence from a priori ratings, geometric interpretability).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation with systematic sensitivity analysis across five subspace selection techniques, four dimensionalities (20, 50, 200, 500), and two context window sizes (2+2, 5+5), yielding 40 distinct model configurations with consistent reporting.

True zero-shot capability for phrase representation: model requires only word-level vectors, not phrase-level co-occurrence statistics, enabling application to novel phrases—genuine practical advantage over Gutiérrez et al. V1/V2.

Intriguing geometric pattern (horseshoe phenomenon) where metaphoric and literal compositions cluster at periphery with ambiguous cases in middle; pattern holds across multiple subspace types (Joint, Independent, Zipped), suggesting potential robustness.

Honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings: authors explicitly state initial surprise at horseshoe phenomenon (contradicting a priori predictions), acknowledge V2 comparison is indirect, and discuss dataset bias in BO predictiveness.
Clear geometric visualizations (Figure 1, Figure 2) effectively communicating the triangulation scheme and metaphoric-literal-ambiguous progression.
limitations: ZERO-SHOT CLAIM IS MISLEADING: The paper claims 'zero-shot' capability, but logistic regression classifier is trained on labeled data from Gutiérrez et al. dataset. Only phrase representation is zero-shot; classification model is supervised. This distinction is not clearly articulated in abstract or introduction, creating misleading framing about true zero-shot learning capability. No explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases; cross-validation uses shuffled folds of same dataset, not truly unseen data.

WEAK INDIVIDUAL GEOMETRIC FEATURES UNDERMINE INTERPRETABILITY CLAIM: Table 3 shows most individual geometric features perform only marginally above majority-class baseline (F≈0.697): AO=0.669, AB=0.644, CE=0.652, DE=0.651, CD=0.651. Only BO (noun norm) achieves notably higher performance (F≈0.739–0.753). Authors acknowledge 'aside from the noun norm BO, very few of the features independently outperform the majority class baseline.' This raises critical question: does combined model's success (F=0.813) reflect genuine geometric meaningfulness or logistic regression's ability to weight weak signals? Ablation studies and non-linear classifier comparison would clarify, but are absent.

HORSESHOE PHENOMENON DISCOVERED POST-HOC WITHOUT A PRIORI PREDICTION OR INDEPENDENT VALIDATION: The horseshoe pattern (metaphoric/literal clustering with ambiguous in middle) is discovered during analysis, not predicted a priori. Authors explicitly state 'We were admittedly initially surprised by this evident bulging at the middle' and acknowledge it contradicts their a priori prediction of 'steady widening and corresponding move towards the periphery.' Pattern is observed on same dataset used for training; no cross-dataset validation or held-out test set evaluation provided. Post-hoc discoveries require independent validation to avoid overfitting to dataset-specific artifacts.

COMPARISON TO GUTIÉRREZ ET AL. V2 IS INDIRECT AND POTENTIALLY MISLEADING: V2 results are reported on reduced dataset (F=0.793), while V1 results are on full dataset (F=0.817). Authors acknowledge V2 full-dataset performance is likely lower than reported 0.793 (lines 501–520). This makes comparison indirect and potentially overstates the proposed method's advantage. Authors note 'Evaluation on the reduced set is not currently possible, as the identity of the subset used is not available' (footnote 1), preventing fair reduced-dataset comparison.

NO CROSS-DATASET EVALUATION; GENERALIZATION TO OTHER METAPHOR TYPES UNCLEAR: Evaluation limited to single dataset (Gutiérrez et al. adjective-noun pairs with 23 adjectives chosen for metaphoric/literal versatility). No evaluation on other metaphor corpora (VU Amsterdam, TroFi), other linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun), or other languages. Generalization to broader metaphor identification tasks is unvalidated. The horseshoe phenomenon is observed only on training dataset; no independent validation on held-out data or cross-dataset evaluation.

THEORETICAL POSITIONING AGAINST CONCEPTUAL MAPPING NOT EMPIRICALLY VALIDATED: The paper asserts that pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theories are more appropriate than conceptual mapping frameworks, but provides no direct empirical test of which theory better predicts human metaphor judgments or processing. No comparison to human processing data (reading times, eye-tracking), psycholinguistic experiments, or explicit tests of theoretical predictions. The theoretical choice is asserted, not validated.
open_questions: ZERO-SHOT CAPABILITY SCOPE: What is the true zero-shot capability when evaluated on held-out unseen phrases not in the training set? Current evaluation uses cross-validation folds of the same dataset. Does the model generalize to adjectives or nouns not seen during training? Can it handle novel adjective-noun combinations beyond the 8,592 pairs in Gutiérrez et al.?

GEOMETRIC FEATURE MEANINGFULNESS: Do the weak individual geometric features (most F≈0.64–0.75) reflect genuine relationships with metaphoricity, or are they statistical artifacts? Would non-linear classifiers (SVM, random forest) perform substantially better, suggesting non-linear feature interactions? What do ablation studies reveal about which feature combinations drive the combined model's performance?

HORSESHOE PHENOMENON GENERALIZATION: Does the horseshoe pattern hold on independent metaphor datasets (VU Amsterdam, TroFi) and other linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun)? Is it a genuine linguistic principle reflecting metaphor as a spectrum, or a dataset-specific artifact of the Gutiérrez et al. design? Can it be predicted a priori from pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory, or is it purely post-hoc?

PRAGMATIC THEORY VALIDATION: Does the model's performance validate pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory over conceptual mapping? How do model predictions compare to human metaphoricity judgments, reading times, or eye-tracking data? Does the geometric framework align with human conceptual organization or pragmatic reasoning protocols?

COMPARISON FAIRNESS: What are the full-dataset results for Gutiérrez et al. V2? Can a fair reduced-dataset comparison be conducted where both methods are evaluated on the same subset? How do confidence intervals and effect sizes compare across methods?

BO FEATURE PREDICTIVENESS: Does BO's (noun norm) high predictiveness reflect a fundamental geometric property of metaphor, or does it reflect dataset bias (adjectives chosen for versatility, nouns less so)? How does BO performance vary on datasets with more balanced adjective and noun versatility?

ALTERNATIVE METHODS COMPARISON: How does the proposed method compare to GloVe, FastText, and contextual embeddings (BERT, RoBERTa)? Do geometric patterns hold across different distributional semantic methods? How does performance compare to non-linear classifiers (SVM, random forest, gradient boosting)?

ANNOTATION QUALITY: What is the inter-annotator agreement for the Gutiérrez et al. dataset? How does model performance vary on high-agreement vs. low-agreement examples? Does annotation ambiguity correlate with the horseshoe phenomenon's intermediate cases?
consensus_snapshot: All five reviewers converge on identifying the same core issues: (1) zero-shot claim is misleading (phrase representation is zero-shot, classification is supervised); (2) horseshoe phenomenon is post-hoc without a priori prediction or independent validation; (3) most individual geometric features perform poorly (F≈0.64–0.75 vs. baseline 0.697); (4) comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 is indirect (reduced dataset); (5) no cross-dataset evaluation limits generalization claims.
All reviewers acknowledge the paper is methodologically sound, theoretically coherent, and makes a controlled contribution to metaphor identification research.
All reviewers recognize the genuine practical advantage of zero-shot phrase representation (no phrase vectors required) over Gutiérrez et al. V1/V2.
All reviewers flag the weak individual geometric features as undermining the interpretability claim, though they differ on implications.
All reviewers note the paper's honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings (e.g., initial surprise at horseshoe phenomenon).
All reviewers agree that the theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics vs. conceptual mapping) is coherent and well-motivated but lacks direct empirical validation.

All reviewers identify the same uncertainty hotspots: horseshoe generalization, geometric feature meaningfulness, zero-shot scope, V2 comparison fairness, theoretical validation, and cross-dataset generalization.

This reflects different weighting of methodological vs. theoretical novelty.

GEOMETRIC INTERPRETABILITY IMPLICATIONS: Reviewers agree weak individual features undermine interpretability claims, but differ on severity. Reviewer_2 (methodology_auditor) treats this as major flaw requiring ablation studies; reviewer_4 (disruptive lens) suggests feature interactions might explain combined success despite weak individual performance.

HORSESHOE PHENOMENON SIGNIFICANCE: Reviewers agree it is post-hoc and lacks validation, but differ on implications. Reviewer_1 (structure_analyst) treats it as logical tension contradicting a priori predictions and undermining theory; reviewer_4 (disruptive lens) treats it as potentially novel emergent finding requiring validation.

ZERO-SHOT CLAIM SEVERITY: All reviewers flag misleading framing, but differ on severity. Reviewer_1 and reviewer_2 treat it as major methodological flaw; reviewer_3 and reviewer_5 treat it as clarity/framing issue requiring clarification rather than fundamental invalidity.

THEORETICAL VALIDATION CRITICALITY: Reviewers agree pragmatic/cognitive linguistic grounding is not empirically validated, but differ on whether this is critical flaw (reviewer_2, reviewer_5) or expected limitation for theoretical positioning (reviewer_4).

INCREMENTAL VS. DISRUPTIVE FRAMING: Reviewer_3 emphasizes incremental methodological contribution building on prior work; reviewer_4 emphasizes novel theoretical positioning as controlled but substantive departure from dominant Lakoff & Johnson framework. Both assessments are defensible depending on how novelty is weighted.
uncertainty_snapshot: HORSESHOE PHENOMENON GENERALIZATION: Post-hoc discovery without a priori prediction or independent validation. Critical uncertainty: Does pattern hold on other metaphor datasets and linguistic constructions, or is it dataset-specific artifact? Does it reflect genuine linguistic principle or model-fitting?

GEOMETRIC FEATURE MEANINGFULNESS: Weak individual feature performance (most F≈0.64–0.75) vs. strong combined model (F=0.813). Critical uncertainty: Does combined success reflect genuine geometric meaningfulness or logistic regression's ability to weight weak signals? Would non-linear classifiers perform better?

ZERO-SHOT CAPABILITY SCOPE: Phrase representation is genuinely zero-shot, but classification model is supervised. Critical uncertainty: What is true zero-shot capability when evaluated on held-out unseen phrases? Current evaluation uses cross-validation folds of same dataset.

COMPARISON TO GUTIÉRREZ ET AL. V2: V2 results on reduced dataset; full-dataset performance unknown. Authors acknowledge V2 full-dataset likely lower than reported 0.793. Critical uncertainty: What is fair comparison when V1 is full-dataset and V2 is reduced-dataset?

THEORETICAL GROUNDING VALIDATION: Pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory is coherent but not empirically tested against human processing data or conceptual mapping baseline. Critical uncertainty: Does model's performance validate pragmatic theory over conceptual mapping, or is theoretical choice independent of empirical results?

GENERALIZATION BEYOND ADJECTIVE-NOUN PAIRS: Evaluation limited to single dataset with 23 adjectives chosen for metaphoric/literal versatility. Critical uncertainty: Does method generalize to verb-noun, noun-noun, other languages, or other metaphor datasets?

ANNOTATION QUALITY EFFECTS: No inter-annotator agreement reported for Gutiérrez et al. dataset. Paper treats binary annotations as ground truth despite asserting metaphor is contextual and ambiguous. Critical uncertainty: How much annotation noise affects performance ceiling and model evaluation?

BO FEATURE PREDICTIVENESS CAUSALITY: BO (noun norm) is most predictive feature, but authors acknowledge this may reflect dataset bias (adjectives chosen for versatility, nouns less so). Critical uncertainty: Does BO predictiveness reflect fundamental geometric property or dataset design artifact?

FEATURE INTERACTION MECHANISMS: Weak individual features but strong combined model suggests feature interactions are important. Critical uncertainty: How do geometric features combine to predict metaphoricity? What is the mechanism of the combined model's success?

STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF IMPROVEMENTS: Paper reports p<0.05 significance using χ² but provides no confidence intervals or effect sizes. Critical uncertainty: Is the 0.004 F-score improvement over V1 (0.813 vs. 0.817) statistically or practically significant?

McGregor et al. (2015) - Methodological foundation for contextual subspace projection; applies to concept discovery rather than metaphor identification. This paper adapts McGregor et al.'s technique to metaphor task.

Agres et al. (2016) - Proposes five subspace selection techniques (Joint, Independent, Zipped, Adjective-Only, Noun-Only) for metaphor perception modeling. This paper expands on Agres et al.'s framework with systematic evaluation.

Wilson & Sperber (2012), Carston (2012), Davidson (1978), Reimer (2001) - Theoretical foundations for pragmatic/contextual view of metaphor. Paper operationalizes these theories computationally through geometric subspace projection.
Lakoff & Johnson (1980) - Dominant conceptual mapping framework for metaphor. Paper explicitly positions itself against this framework, arguing for pragmatic/contextual alternative.
McElree & Nordlie (1999), Wolff & Gentner (2011) - Psycholinguistic evidence of neurological ambiguity in metaphor processing. Cited to support claim that metaphor is dynamic and contextual.

Li et al. (TACL) - Data-driven metaphor recognition using knowledge-base and probabilistic methods. Retrieved literature emphasizes data-driven and knowledge-base approaches but does not directly address pragmatic/cognitive linguistic framing or geometric interpretability claims.
Sahlgren (2008) - Theoretical support for semantic vs. syntactic trade-off in distributional semantics. Cited to explain why larger context windows (5+5) outperform smaller windows (2+2).
ARR Reviewer Guidelines - Common problems in NLP papers; used to structure evaluation of methodological rigor, statistical reporting, and claim support.
transparency_notes: Five specialist reviewers with distinct cognitive roles (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive, claim_verifier) were applied to the paper. Each reviewer operated within their assigned epistemic variant without recommending accept/reject decisions.

Reviewers converged on identifying the same core issues across diverse analytical perspectives, suggesting these are robust concerns rather than artifacts of particular viewpoints. This convergence provides confidence in the identified limitations.

Reviewers diverged on severity and implications of identified issues, reflecting legitimate differences in how to weight methodological rigor, novelty, and empirical support. The controlled disagreement is preserved in the consensus/disagreement snapshots.

The paper's theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics vs. conceptual mapping) is novel and coherent but not empirically validated. Reviewers agree this is a gap but differ on whether it is critical flaw or expected limitation for theoretical positioning.

The horseshoe phenomenon is treated as intriguing but uncertain by all reviewers. The post-hoc discovery without a priori prediction raises questions about generalization, but does not invalidate the finding. Independent validation would clarify whether this is genuine linguistic principle or dataset artifact.

The weak individual geometric features are flagged by all reviewers as undermining the interpretability claim. However, reviewers differ on implications: some treat this as evidence that combined model reflects logistic regression weighting; others suggest feature interactions might explain combined success. Ablation studies would clarify this.

The zero-shot claim is flagged by all reviewers as misleading because it conflates phrase representation (zero-shot) with classification (supervised). This is a clarity/framing issue, not a validity issue. Clarification and explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases would resolve this concern.

The comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 is flagged by all reviewers as indirect because V2 results are on reduced dataset while V1 results are on full dataset. This is a methodological concern about fair comparison, not a validity concern about the proposed method.

Retrieved literature (Li et al., TACL) on metaphor recognition emphasizes data-driven and knowledge-base approaches but does not directly address the pragmatic/cognitive linguistic framing or geometric interpretability claims. This reflects the novelty of the paper's theoretical positioning.

The paper demonstrates honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings (e.g., authors acknowledge initial surprise at horseshoe phenomenon, acknowledge V2 comparison is indirect). This transparency is commendable but does not fully resolve the underlying issues.

Epistemic limits are explicitly documented: theoretical validation requires human processing data; generalization scope is limited to single dataset; geometric interpretability cannot be definitively established without ablation studies; horseshoe causality is unclear; zero-shot scope is limited by evaluation methodology; comparison fairness is compromised by dataset mismatch; annotation quality is unknown; alternative methods are not compared; pragmatic reasoning alignment is not validated; dataset bias effects are not isolated; statistical significance is not fully reported; feature interaction mechanisms are not analyzed.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a coherent and methodologically sound contribution with novel theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics) and practical advantages (zero-shot phrase representation, interpretability). However, several claims require clarification or additional evidence before publication at a top-tier venue. MAJOR REVISIONS REQUIRED: (1) Clarify zero-shot claim by distinguishing phrase representation (zero-shot) from classification (supervised). Conduct explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases to validate true zero-shot capability. (2) Validate horseshoe phenomenon on independent dataset (held-out test set or cross-dataset evaluation). Provide a priori theoretical justification for why horseshoe should emerge from pragmatic/cognitive linguistic principles. (3) Conduct ablation studies and non-linear classifier comparison to validate that weak individual geometric features reflect genuine relationships rather than artifacts. Provide feature importance analysis (SHAP values). (4) Obtain full-dataset Gutiérrez et al. V2 results or conduct fair reduced-dataset comparison. Report confidence intervals and effect sizes for all comparisons. (5) Evaluate on additional metaphor datasets (VU Amsterdam, TroFi) and linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun) to assess generalization. (6) Conduct human evaluation comparing model predictions to human metaphoricity judgments. Test whether pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory better predicts human behavior than conceptual mapping. (7) Report inter-annotator agreement for Gutiérrez et al. dataset. Provide detailed methodology for χ² test. Report confidence intervals and effect sizes. (8) Compare to alternative distributional methods (GloVe, FastText, contextual embeddings) and non-linear classifiers. DECISION: The paper is suitable for publication with major revisions addressing these issues. The contribution is incremental methodologically but potentially disruptive theoretically, contingent on validation of pragmatic/cognitive linguistic framing. The work would benefit from cross-dataset evaluation and human studies to strengthen claims about metaphor as a dynamic contextual phenomenon. The honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings is commendable and should be preserved in revision.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a controlled but substantive contribution to metaphor identification research. To strengthen the work and address reviewer concerns, prioritize the following revisions: (1) ZERO-SHOT CLAIM: Clarify that phrase representation is zero-shot but classification is supervised. Conduct explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases (not just cross-validation folds) to validate true zero-shot capability. Report performance separately for seen vs. unseen adjectives/nouns. (2) GEOMETRIC INTERPRETABILITY: Conduct ablation studies removing individual features to assess their contribution. Test non-linear classifiers (SVM with RBF kernel, random forest, gradient boosting) to determine whether weak individual features reflect genuine relationships or model limitation. Provide feature importance analysis (SHAP values) to clarify which geometric properties drive predictions. (3) HORSESHOE PHENOMENON: Validate on independent dataset (other metaphor corpus or held-out test set). Provide a priori theoretical justification for why horseshoe should emerge from pragmatic/cognitive linguistic principles. Conduct statistical significance testing of the trend (e.g., linear regression on ratio vs. metaphoricity category). (4) COMPARISON TO BASELINES: Obtain full-dataset Gutiérrez et al. V2 results or conduct fair reduced-dataset comparison. Report 95% confidence intervals for all F-scores. Calculate effect sizes (Cohen's h for proportions). Conduct paired t-test or McNemar's test for comparing model performance. (5) THEORETICAL VALIDATION: Conduct human evaluation comparing model predictions to human metaphoricity judgments. Test whether pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory better predicts human behavior than conceptual mapping. Use eye-tracking or fMRI data if available. (6) GENERALIZATION: Evaluate on additional metaphor datasets (VU Amsterdam Metaphor Corpus, TroFi dataset). Test on other linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun, prepositional phrases). Report performance across dataset types and linguistic constructions. (7) STATISTICAL REPORTING: Report inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa) for Gutiérrez et al. dataset. Provide detailed methodology for χ² test. Report confidence intervals and effect sizes for all comparisons. Apply multiple comparisons correction if testing multiple hypotheses. (8) ALTERNATIVE METHODS: Compare to GloVe, FastText, and contextual embeddings (BERT, RoBERTa). Compare to non-linear classifiers (SVM, random forest, gradient boosting). Report results in comparison table. (9) DATASET BIAS ANALYSIS: Evaluate model performance on balanced dataset where adjectives and nouns are equally versatile. Analyze whether BO's predictiveness reflects dataset design or genuine geometric property. (10) FEATURE INTERACTION ANALYSIS: Analyze feature interactions to understand why combined model performs well despite weak individual features. Consider non-linear feature interactions or feature combinations that might be more interpretable. These revisions would significantly strengthen the empirical support for your claims and clarify the scope and limitations of your contribution. The honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings should be preserved and expanded in revision.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes a geometric, context-sensitive distributional semantic model for metaphor identification in adjective-noun phrases, grounded in pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory (Wilson & Sperber, Carston, Davidson) rather than conceptual mapping frameworks (Lakoff & Johnson). The core methodological contribution is using contextually-projected geometric subspaces of word vectors to extract features for logistic regression classification. The paper claims: (1) metaphors are dynamic contextual phenomena, (2) contextual subspace projection enables zero-shot metaphor identification without phrase-level training data, (3) geometric properties (triangle side lengths) correlate with metaphoricity, (4) performance is comparable to supervised baselines (F=0.813 vs. Gutiérrez et al. V1=0.817), and (5) a 'horseshoe phenomenon' exists where metaphoric and literal phrases cluster geometrically with ambiguous cases in between. Five specialist reviewers with distinct cognitive roles converge on identifying critical gaps between claims and evidence, while disagreeing on severity and implications.

Strengths:
- Coherent theoretical motivation grounded in pragmatic/cognitive linguistics with explicit rejection of conceptual mapping as sole framework; well-articulated positioning against dominant Lakoff & Johnson tradition.
- Methodologically simple and interpretable geometric framework using triangulation in contextual subspaces; clear mathematical formulation and explicit operationalization of three desiderata (contextual selection, independence from a priori ratings, geometric interpretability).
- Comprehensive empirical evaluation with systematic sensitivity analysis across five subspace selection techniques, four dimensionalities (20, 50, 200, 500), and two context window sizes (2+2, 5+5), yielding 40 distinct model configurations.
- True zero-shot capability for phrase representation: model requires only word-level vectors, not phrase-level co-occurrence statistics, enabling application to novel phrases—genuine practical advantage over Gutiérrez et al. V1/V2.
- Intriguing geometric pattern (horseshoe phenomenon) where metaphoric and literal compositions cluster at periphery with ambiguous cases in middle; pattern holds across multiple subspace types (Joint, Independent, Zipped).
- Honest acknowledgment of limitations and surprising findings: authors explicitly state initial surprise at horseshoe phenomenon (contradicting a priori predictions), acknowledge V2 comparison is indirect, and discuss dataset bias in BO predictiveness.

Limitations:
- ZERO-SHOT CLAIM IS MISLEADING: The paper claims 'zero-shot' capability, but logistic regression classifier is trained on labeled data. Only phrase representation is zero-shot; classification model is supervised. This distinction is not clearly articulated, creating misleading framing. No explicit evaluation on held-out unseen phrases; cross-validation uses shuffled folds of same dataset.
- WEAK INDIVIDUAL GEOMETRIC FEATURES UNDERMINE INTERPRETABILITY CLAIM: Table 3 shows most individual geometric features perform only marginally above majority-class baseline (F≈0.697): AO=0.669, AB=0.644, CE=0.652, DE=0.651, CD=0.651. Only BO achieves notably higher performance (F≈0.739–0.753). Authors acknowledge 'aside from the noun norm BO, very few of the features independently outperform the majority class baseline.' This raises critical question: does combined model's success (F=0.813) reflect genuine geometric meaningfulness or logistic regression's ability to weight weak signals?
- HORSESHOE PHENOMENON DISCOVERED POST-HOC WITHOUT A PRIORI PREDICTION OR INDEPENDENT VALIDATION: The horseshoe pattern is discovered during analysis, not predicted a priori. Authors explicitly state 'We were admittedly initially surprised by this evident bulging at the middle' and acknowledge it contradicts their a priori prediction of 'steady widening and corresponding move towards the periphery.' Pattern is observed on same dataset used for training; no cross-dataset validation or held-out test set evaluation provided.
- COMPARISON TO GUTIÉRREZ ET AL. V2 IS INDIRECT AND POTENTIALLY MISLEADING: V2 results are reported on reduced dataset (F=0.793), while V1 results are on full dataset (F=0.817). Authors acknowledge V2 full-dataset performance is likely lower than reported 0.793. This makes comparison indirect and potentially overstates the proposed method's advantage.
- NO CROSS-DATASET EVALUATION; GENERALIZATION TO OTHER METAPHOR TYPES UNCLEAR: Evaluation limited to single dataset (Gutiérrez et al. adjective-noun pairs with 23 adjectives chosen for metaphoric/literal versatility). No evaluation on other metaphor corpora (VU Amsterdam, TroFi), other linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun), or other languages. Generalization to broader metaphor identification tasks is unvalidated.

Open Questions:
- ZERO-SHOT CAPABILITY SCOPE: What is the true zero-shot capability when evaluated on held-out unseen phrases not in the training set? Current evaluation uses cross-validation folds of the same dataset. Does the model generalize to adjectives or nouns not seen during training?
- GEOMETRIC FEATURE MEANINGFULNESS: Do the weak individual geometric features reflect genuine relationships with metaphoricity, or are they statistical artifacts? Would non-linear classifiers (SVM, random forest) perform substantially better, suggesting non-linear feature interactions? What do ablation studies reveal about which feature combinations drive the combined model's performance?
- HORSESHOE PHENOMENON GENERALIZATION: Does the horseshoe pattern hold on independent metaphor datasets (VU Amsterdam, TroFi) and other linguistic constructions (verb-noun, noun-noun)? Is it a genuine linguistic principle reflecting metaphor as a spectrum, or a dataset-specific artifact?
- PRAGMATIC THEORY VALIDATION: Does the model's performance validate pragmatic/cognitive linguistic theory over conceptual mapping? How do model predictions compare to human metaphoricity judgments, reading times, or eye-tracking data? Does the geometric framework align with human conceptual organization or pragmatic reasoning protocols?

Transparency:
- Five specialist reviewers with distinct cognitive roles (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive, claim_verifier) were applied to the paper. Each reviewer operated within their assigned epistemic variant without recommending accept/reject decisions.
- Reviewers converged on identifying the same core issues across diverse analytical perspectives: zero-shot claim is misleading, horseshoe is post-hoc, weak individual features undermine interpretability, V2 comparison is indirect, no cross-dataset evaluation. This convergence suggests these are robust concerns.
- Reviewers diverged on severity and implications, reflecting legitimate differences in how to weight methodological rigor, novelty, and empirical support. The controlled disagreement is preserved in consensus/disagreement snapshots.
- The paper's theoretical positioning (pragmatic/cognitive linguistics vs. conceptual mapping) is novel and coherent but not empirically validated. Reviewers agree this is a gap but differ on whether it is critical flaw or expected limitation.
- Epistemic limits are explicitly documented: theoretical validation requires human processing data; generalization scope is limited to single dataset; geometric interpretability cannot be definitively established without ablation studies; horseshoe causality is unclear; zero-shot scope is limited by evaluation methodology; comparison fairness is compromised by dataset mismatch; annotation quality is unknown; alternative methods are not compared; pragmatic reasoning alignment is not validated; dataset bias effects are not isolated; statistical significance is not fully reported; feature interaction mechanisms are not analyzed.

We utter about one metaphor for every ten to twenty-ﬁve words, or about six metaphors a minute (Geary, 2011). Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

The selection restriction the- ory (Wilks, 1978) argues that the meaning of an ex- pression is restricted by its context, and violations of the restriction imply a metaphor. Resnik (1993) uses KL divergence to measure the selectional preference strength (SPS) , i.e., how strongly a context restricts an expression. Although he did not use this measure directly for metaphor recognition, SPS (and also a related measure called the selection association) is widely used in more re- cent approaches for metaphor recognition and inter- pretation (Mason, 2004; Shutova, 2010; Shutova et al., 2010; Baumer et al., 2010). As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).
